examples.question: A charity packs 96 stationery kits. The numbers of red and blue kits are in the ratio 5:3. Calculate how many kits of each colour there are. Show your working.
examples.solution: There are 5+3=8 equal parts. Each part is 96÷8=12. Red = 5×12=60 kits and blue = 3×12=36 kits. Check 60+36=96 and 60:36=5:3.

criteria.description: Correctly identify 8 equal parts or an equivalent proportional representation.
criteria.missingFeedback: Add the ratio parts before dividing the total. A 5:3 split has eight equal parts.

criteria.description: Find 96÷8=12 or apply a correct equivalent method.
criteria.missingFeedback: Divide the total kits by the eight equal ratio parts.

criteria.description: 60 red kits from valid red-share calculation.
criteria.missingFeedback: Multiply the value of one part by five; check the unit is kits.

criteria.description: 36 blue kits, independently correct by any valid method.
criteria.missingFeedback: Use three equal parts or subtract the red share from the total, then check the ratio.

examples.topic: Intersections of linear and quadratic graphs
examples.question: The curves y=x²−3x−4 and y=x+2 intersect at two points. Find the exact coordinates of both intersection points. Show your algebra.
examples.solution: Equating the two expressions gives x²−3x−4=x+2, so x²−4x−6=0. By the quadratic formula, x=(4±√(16+24))/2=2±√10. Substitution into y=x+2 gives y=4±√10. Coordinates are (2+√10,4+√10) and (2−√10,4−√10), with matching signs. Check in both equations.

criteria.description: Set both y expressions equal and obtain x²−4x−6=0 or equivalent.
criteria.missingFeedback: At an intersection, both equations have the same x and y values; equate the expressions for y.

criteria.description: Apply the quadratic formula or an equivalent exact method to the resulting equation.
criteria.missingFeedback: Use a reliable quadratic method and check the discriminant before simplifying.
Simplify √40 as 2√10, then divide the entire numerator by two.

criteria.description: Substitute both x-values into y=x+2 or the quadratic relationship.
criteria.missingFeedback: Substitute each root back into either original expression to find its matching y-value.

criteria.description: Give both exact coordinates with corresponding ± signs correctly matched.
criteria.missingFeedback: Keep the plus-root y-coordinate with the plus-root x-coordinate, and likewise for minus.

examples.topic: Differentiation and classification of stationary points
examples.question: For y=x³−6x²+9x+1, determine every stationary point and classify each as a local maximum or local minimum. Show how your classification follows.
examples.solution: dy/dx=3x²−12x+9=3(x−1)(x−3). Hence x=1 or x=3. At x=1, y=5; at x=3, y=1. Also d²y/dx²=6x−12. At x=1, d²y/dx²=−6, giving a local maximum (1,5). At x=3, d²y/dx²=6, giving a local minimum (3,1). A correct derivative-sign test is an alternative classification method.

criteria.description: Obtain 3x²−12x+9 or an equivalent first derivative.
criteria.missingFeedback: Differentiate each power term and remember the constant differentiates to zero.

criteria.description: Set a first derivative equal to zero and solve the resulting quadratic.
criteria.missingFeedback: Stationary points satisfy dy/dx=0; factor the derivative and solve.
Check the factors of the derivative to find both x-values.

criteria.description: Evaluate y at both stationary x-values using the original equation.
criteria.missingFeedback: Substitute each stationary x-value into y, not dy/dx, to obtain both points.
Recheck the powers and signs in y when calculating the coordinates.

criteria.skill: Classify the nature of both points
criteria.description: Correctly identify (1,5) as a local maximum and (3,1) as a local minimum from a valid derivative-sign or second-derivative argument.
criteria.missingFeedback: Use the second derivative or derivative sign changes to justify maximum and minimum.
